title: Ask how the business makes money first, because its business model decides where the problem hides
description: The common ways companies earn money, from selling products to subscriptions, marketplaces and advertising, and what each means for a case.
hook: One of the most useful questions you can ask at the start of any case is simply: how does this business make money? Many candidates skip it because it feels too basic. It is not. The way a company earns its money decides which numbers matter, where problems usually hide, and which ideas will actually work. Here are the models you will meet most often, explained simply.
body:
1. Selling products

The simplest model: make or buy something, sell it for more than it cost. A bakery, a car maker, a clothing shop. Profit comes from volume × (price − cost per unit), minus fixed costs like rent. In a case, look at how many units are sold, at what price, and what each one costs to make.

2. Selling services by the hour or project

Law firms, agencies, builders and consultancies sell people's time. Revenue is roughly people × hours billed × rate. The key number is utilisation: how much of their paid time staff spend on work clients pay for. A firm with idle staff loses money fast, because salaries are a fixed cost.

3. Subscriptions

Customers pay every month or year: streaming, software, gyms, phone contracts. What matters is how many customers join, how much each pays, and how long they stay. A small change in churn (the share who cancel) has a big effect over time. If 5% leave each month, the average customer stays about 20 months; cut that to 2.5% and they stay about 40 months, doubling what each customer is worth.

4. Marketplaces and platforms

Companies like ride-hailing apps, food delivery apps and online marketplaces connect buyers and sellers and take a cut, often called the take rate. They need both sides: riders want lots of drivers, drivers want lots of riders. That is why these businesses often spend heavily early on to grow both sides. See network effects and platforms.

5. Advertising

The user pays nothing; advertisers pay to reach them. Search engines, social media and free news sites work this way. Revenue is roughly users × time spent × ads shown × price per ad. In a case, anything that reduces engagement reduces revenue, even if users never pay a penny.

6. Freemium

A free version attracts lots of users, and a small share pay for a better version. Many apps and software tools work like this. The critical number is the conversion rate from free to paid, and whether free users cost much to serve.

7. Razor and blades

Sell the main product cheaply, then make money on the refills: printers and ink, coffee machines and pods, game consoles and games. In a case, the profit is in the repeat purchase, so losing control of the refills (to cheaper copies, for example) is a serious threat.

8. Licensing and franchising

The company lets others use its brand, recipe or technology in return for a fee or a share of sales. Many fast-food chains are mostly franchised. The company earns less per shop but takes far less risk and needs far less money to grow.

How to use this in a case

Ask how the client makes money in your clarifying questions. Then let the answer shape your structure: for a subscription business, split revenue into new customers, retained customers and price; for a marketplace, look at both sides and the take rate. A structure built around the real business model always sounds sharper than a generic "revenue and costs".
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case.
